title: Materials in Products Selection: Tools for Including User-Interaction in Materials Selection

findings.antecedent: Product designer using 'own method' for materials selection
findings.consequent: Product designer's certainty about starting an effective materials search
findings.mechanism: The 'own method' is familiar and established for designers, leading to higher confidence in their approach.
findings.quote: When the product designers used their own method, they more often increased their certainty compared to when they used one of the offered tools.

findings.antecedent: Use of Sample tool or Question tool for materials selection
findings.consequent: Increase in certainty about starting an effective materials search
findings.mechanism: These tools were less effective in providing clear guidance or concrete outcomes for materials search, leading to lower confidence.
findings.quote: The sample and question tools are least effective in increasing certainty.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool for materials selection
findings.consequent: Decrease in certainty about starting an effective materials search
findings.mechanism: The visual nature of the picture tool might provide enough clarity to prevent a decrease in certainty, even if not always increasing it.
findings.quote: The picture tool never resulted in a decrease of certainty

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool for materials selection
findings.consequent: Maintaining same certainty about starting an effective materials search
findings.mechanism: The picture tool provided a stable reference point, helping participants maintain their initial level of certainty.
findings.quote: this tool also scored the highest in keeping the same certainty.

findings.antecedent: Use of Sample tool or Question tool by students
findings.consequent: Decrease in certainty about starting an effective materials search
findings.mechanism: Students, lacking experience, found these tools less effective in providing clear direction, leading to reduced confidence.
findings.quote: The sample and question tools led to a decrease in certainty more often than the other tools, especially for students.

findings.antecedent: Use of MiPS tools (Picture, Sample, Question) or 'own method' for materials selection
findings.consequent: Agreement on sensorial properties between clients and product designers (number of similar terms out of 5)
findings.mechanism: Despite tool use, inherent subjectivity in defining sensorial properties limited consensus, with agreement ranging from 1 to 3 terms.
findings.quote: In general, we found limited agreement on sensorial properties between the profiles made by clients and product designers (Table 9).

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool or Question tool (especially after 'own method')
findings.consequent: Number of common sensorial properties agreed upon by clients and product designers
findings.mechanism: These tools provided structured prompts or visual references that facilitated shared understanding and articulation of sensorial properties.
findings.quote: The picture and question tools led to the largest number of properties common to both clients and product designers.

findings.antecedent: Decrease in certainty after using Sample tool (4 times) or Question tool (1 time)
findings.consequent: Level of consensus on key sensorial properties
findings.mechanism: Uncertainty in the design process, particularly after using less effective tools, hindered the ability of participants to reach agreement on material properties.
findings.quote: When participants were uncertain after using the sample tool, it thus led to a low level of consensus.

findings.antecedent: Use of Question tool
findings.consequent: Product designers' profiles described in sensorial properties
findings.mechanism: The structured questions explicitly guided discussions towards sensory aspects, facilitating the translation of abstract user-interaction into concrete sensorial terms.
findings.quote: The question tool directed to sensorial properties mostly.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool or Sample tool
findings.consequent: Product designers' profiles described in sensorial properties
findings.mechanism: These tools, while providing visual and tactile input, lacked a clear translation step, causing discussions to remain at a perceptual level rather than converting to specific sensorial properties.
findings.quote: The picture and sample tools did stay on the perceptual level in one third to one half of the cases.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool
findings.consequent: Time required to get familiar with the tool
findings.mechanism: The visual and intuitive nature of the picture tool made it easy to understand and use quickly.
findings.quote: the picture tool required the least amount of time to get familiar with

findings.antecedent: Use of Question tool
findings.consequent: Time required to get familiar with the tool and use in design brief meetings
findings.mechanism: The structured and detailed nature of the question tool required more cognitive effort and time for participants to navigate and apply effectively in discussions.
findings.quote: the question tool took the longest in design brief meetings.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool
findings.consequent: Overall usability rating
findings.mechanism: Its visual and intuitive nature made it easy to understand and apply, contributing to high user satisfaction.
findings.quote: the picture tool was rated as most usable overall.

findings.antecedent: Use of Question tool
findings.consequent: Overall usability rating
findings.mechanism: Its structured and potentially rigid format made it less adaptable and harder to use in a conversational setting.
findings.quote: The question tool was rated as least usable

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool
findings.consequent: Inspiration level and generation of new ideas
findings.mechanism: The diverse product examples and personalities presented visually stimulated creative thinking and idea generation.
findings.quote: The picture tool was judged as very inspiring by the majority of the participants, because it led to new ideas quickly.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool
findings.consequent: Creativity restriction ('out-of-the-box' thinking)
findings.mechanism: The abundance of specific examples might inadvertently limit divergent thinking by anchoring participants to existing solutions.
findings.quote: Drawbacks of the picture tool were that it makes it hard to think 'out-of-the-box'

findings.antecedent: Use of Sample tool by professional participants
findings.consequent: Inspiration level
findings.mechanism: Professionals, with their experience, could implicitly derive inspiration from tactile interaction with samples, even if not consciously aware.
findings.quote: The professional participants found the sample tool inspiring, although only on an unconscious level.

findings.antecedent: Use of Sample tool by student participants
findings.consequent: Inspiration level
findings.mechanism: Students found it difficult to visualize how raw material samples would translate into a final product, limiting their inspiration.
findings.quote: The student participants, on the other hand, did not find the sample tool inspiring.

findings.antecedent: Use of Question tool
findings.consequent: Inspiration level
findings.mechanism: While clarifying, the structured and directive nature of the questions might not foster spontaneous creative thought.
findings.quote: The question tool was not found inspiring by most participants

findings.antecedent: Use of Question tool
findings.consequent: Clarification and directing of the project approach
findings.mechanism: The structured questions provided a clear framework, helping participants to systematically explore different aspects of the design problem.
findings.quote: although they found the tool clarifying. It helped the participants to approach the project from another angle.

findings.antecedent: Use of MiPS tools by professionals
findings.consequent: Creativity
findings.mechanism: Professionals integrated the tools with their own methods, using them to enhance and structure their creative process.
findings.quote: the professionals' creativity was stimulated in their creativity

findings.antecedent: Use of MiPS tools by students
findings.consequent: Creativity
findings.mechanism: Students perceived the tools as rigid and restrictive, hindering their exploratory creative process.
findings.quote: the students' creativity was restricted.

findings.antecedent: Use of Picture tool or Sample tool vs. Question tool
findings.consequent: Creativity
findings.mechanism: The visual and tactile nature of the picture and sample tools provided more open-ended inspiration compared to the directive question tool.
findings.quote: The picture and sample tools scored better on this issue than the question tool.

findings.antecedent: Availability of MiPS tools (Picture, Sample, Question)
findings.consequent: Preference for working with a combination of tools
findings.mechanism: Participants recognized that different tools addressed different aspects of the design process, making a combined approach more comprehensive.
findings.quote: All but one of the 24 participants preferred to work with a combination of tools.

findings.antecedent: Specific combination of MiPS tools (Picture + Sample, or Picture + Sample + Question)
findings.consequent: Preference for tool combination
findings.mechanism: The combination of visual and tactile input (Picture + Sample) was highly valued, with the addition of structured questioning (Question tool) also being preferred by some.
findings.quote: The most preferred combination was the picture tool together with the sample tool, followed by a combination of all three.

Set of 11 (later 16) physical material samples representing a wide range of sensorial properties.

Summary of tool performance across aspects like increased certainty, consensus about key properties, and profile in sensorial properties.

limitations: The picture cards will vary somewhat depending on culture, trends, and time, and their connection to personality terms might differ in other contexts.
Participants used the tools without any preparation, whereas in practice, designers would prepare before client meetings.
The initial set of material samples was not judged as very inspiring by participants, and some samples were perceived as missing.
The tools were evaluated individually, and none scored high on all desired performances, suggesting a combined form is needed.
Not every tool effectively directed discussions to sensorial properties, sometimes remaining at a perceptual level.

Students, lacking experience, found the tools more restricting to creativity and had more trouble using them than professionals, potentially due to not yet encountering the problems the tools aim to solve or differing approaches to creativity in an educational vs. applied setting.
